The Past Continuous Tense vs. The Simple Past Tense

You use the Past Continuous tense to talk about an action that was happening (in progress) at a time before now.

You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.

You can use the Past Continuous to describe the background in a story written in the past tense.
You often use the Simple Past and the Past Continuous together. You can use the Past Continuous to to describe an action that was interrupted by another event or action (Simple Past).
"I was turning right into a quiet side street, and he just appeared!"
The form of the Past Continuous is:
Last Wednesday, a car hit an eighteen-year-old in-line skater.
While I was talking to Janice Marcus, the head of Skaters for Safety, she said that she was afraid that laws were going to limit the freedom of in-line skaters.
She told me that Skaters for Safety was organizing a skaters' march to show that they wanted a fair shake.
I'm just glad I was wearing a helmet.
The Present Perfect Tense vs. The Simple Past Tense

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.

You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experience.
When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.

For example:

I have learned English. = I learned English in the past and now I can speak English.
In-line skating has become a popular form of transportation. = Inline skating began to be popular in the past and is now popular.

It is common to use for and since when referring to time periods in the Present Perfect:

  • You use FOR to talk about how long an action has been happening (a week, 2 days, five hours, six years etc.)
  • You use SINCE to talk about when the action started (2010, Monday, she was a child)


Usually, when you use the Simple Past tense, the time of the finished action is clear from the context or explicitly mentioned in the sentence.

For example:

Yesterday, I went to the store.
We started discussing this in September.

It is clear when the action occurred. In this sentence we would not use the Present Perfect. (Yesterday, I have been to the store).

images.text:
Last Wednesday, a car hit an eighteen-year-old in-line skater. "I was turning right into a quiet side street, and he just appeared!" exclaimed the driver, "I've never had an accident in my life, and today I put someone in the hospital."

In-line skating, also called rollerblading, has become a popular form of transportation on city streets. However, skating has also been the cause of many road accidents in the past couple of years.

"This has become a serious safety problem in the city," stated the mayor. "We haven't passed any specific laws connected to skating. We haven't decided which traffic laws skaters must obey. We started discussing this in September but haven't made any decisions yet."

While I was talking to Janice Marcus, the head of Skaters for Safety, she said that she was afraid that laws were going to limit the freedom of in-line skaters. She told me that Skaters for Safety was organizing a skaters' march to show that they wanted a fair shake.

James Hiro, the skater injured in last Wednesday's accident, said he was angrier at himself than at the driver and admitted he should have been more careful. "I've been skating for the past two years, and, believe me, I've had many close shaves,” he said.” I'm just glad I was wearing a helmet.”
